claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section with citation and supported by Figure 1C-E.

claims.claim: By late L1, few synapses had formed in the dorsal processes of DDs in pan-1(gk142) mutants.
claims.source: By late L1, few synapses had formed in the dorsal processes of DDs in pan-1(gk142) mutants (Figure 1D,E), indicating that the synaptic remodeling was defective in pan-1 mutants.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 1D,E showing synaptic marker images.

claims.claim: Synaptic remodeling was defective in pan-1 mutants.
claims.source: By late L1, few synapses had formed in the dorsal processes of DDs in pan-1(gk142) mutants (Figure 1D,E), indicating that the synaptic remodeling was defective in pan-1 mutants.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 1D,E.

claims.claim: Axon morphology of DDs in pan-1(gk142) was no different from control animals.
claims.source: Axon morphology of DDs in pan-1(gk142) was no different from control animals; if anything, the GFP intensity of dorsal processes in pan-1(gk142) appeared to be weaker (Figure 1F).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 1F.

claims.claim: The defective synaptic rewiring in pan-1(gk142) had not improved by the end of L2 (28 post-hatch hours).
claims.source: The defective synpatic rewiring had not improved by the end of L2 (28 post-hatch hours) (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 1D.

claims.claim: The loss of pan-1 does not generally affect synaptogenesis in DDs.
claims.source: The presence of juvenile DD synapses in pan-1 mutants suggests that the loss of pan-1 does not generally affect synaptogenesis in DDs.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section as an inference from the observation of ventral synapses.

claims.claim: pan-1 is expressed broadly in embryos and larvae.
claims.source: pan-1 is expressed broadly in embryos and larvae (Gao et al., 2012; Gissendanner and Kelley, 2013).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section with citation to prior work.

claims.claim: Expression of pan-1b driven by unc-25pro restored the synaptic remodeling defects in pan-1 mutants.
claims.source: Expression of longest isoform pan-1b driven by unc-25pro (expressed in DD and VD) restored the synaptic remodeling defects in pan-1 mutants, while the other two isoforms, pan-1a or pan-1c could not (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 2B.

claims.claim: pan-1a and pan-1c isoforms could not restore the synaptic remodeling defects in pan-1 mutants.
claims.source: Expression of longest isoform pan-1b driven by unc-25pro (expressed in DD and VD) restored the synaptic remodeling defects in pan-1 mutants, while the other two isoforms, pan-1a or pan-1c could not (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Expression of pan-1 driven by flp-13pro rescued synaptic rewiring defects in pan-1 mutants.
claims.source: Furthermore, expression of pan-1 (referring to pan-1b hereafter) driven by flp-13pro (expressed in DD not VD among ventral cord motor neurons) also rescued synaptic rewiring defects in pan-1 mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Specific expression of pan-1 in muscles, epidermis, or intestine did not mitigate the deficient synaptic remodeling in pan-1(0).
claims.source: In contrast, specific expression of pan-1 in muscles, epidermis, or intestine did not mitigate the deficient synaptic remodeling in pan-1(0) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: PAN-1B regulates synaptic remodeling in DDs cell autonomously.
claims.source: Together, these data demonstrate that a transmembrane isoform of PAN-1, PAN-1B, regulates synaptic remodeling in DDs cell autonomously; in other words, restoring PAN-1 in DDs is sufficient to promote synaptic rewiring in developmentally arrested mutants.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from rescue experiments.

claims.claim: PAN-1GFP signal was detected broadly in embryos and early larvae, but decreased substantially in late larvae and adults.
claims.source: PAN-1GFP signal was detected broadly in embryos and early larvae, but decreased substantially in late larvae and adults (Figure 3A; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Two types of PAN-1GFP subcellular patterns were observed: at the cell membrane and as cytoplasmic puncta.
claims.source: Two types of PAN-1GFP subcellular patterns were observed: at the cell membrane and as cytoplasmic puncta.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claims.claim: PAN-1 distributed at the lateral basal membrane of seam cells.
claims.source: By colabelling a tight-junction component DLG-1::RFP and PAN-1GFP (Figure 3B), we observed that PAN-1 distributed at the lateral basal membrane of seam cells.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 3B showing colocalization.

claims.claim: PAN-1 is localized on the cell membrane of many ventral cord neurons, including DD neurons at L1 and L2.
claims.source: PAN-1 is also localized on the cell membrane of many ventral cord neurons, including DD neurons at L1 and L2 (Figure 3C,D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 3C,D.

claims.claim: Deleting either the SP or TMD of PAN-1 caused PAN-1 to lose its rescuing activity.
claims.source: Deleting either the SP or TMD caused PAN-1 to lose its rescuing activity, suggesting that PAN-1's membrane localization is required for its function.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claims.claim: PAN-1's membrane localization is required for its function.
claims.source: Deleting either the SP or TMD caused PAN-1 to lose its rescuing activity, suggesting that PAN-1's membrane localization is required for its function.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section as an inference from deletion experiments.

claims.claim: The cytoplasmic region of PAN-1 was not essential for its function.
claims.source: We found that the cytoplasmic region of PAN-1 was not essential for its function; in contrast, the LRR domains, the main motifs within the extracellular region, were necessary for PAN-1's activity in synaptic remodeling.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claims.claim: The LRR domains of PAN-1 were necessary for PAN-1's activity in synaptic remodeling.
claims.source: We found that the cytoplasmic region of PAN-1 was not essential for its function; in contrast, the LRR domains, the main motifs within the extracellular region, were necessary for PAN-1's activity in synaptic remodeling.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claims.claim: In early L1 larvae, MYRF-1GFP signal was observed at the cell membrane of many cell types, but were not obviously enriched in the cytoplasm or nucleus.
claims.source: In early L1 larvae, GFP signal was observed at the cell membrane of many cell types, including pharynx, epidermis, and neurons, but were not obviously enriched in the cytoplasm or nucleus (Figure 4B,C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 4B,C.

claims.claim: Toward late L1 stage, MYRF-1GFP signals started to appear in the nucleus.
claims.source: Toward late L1 stage, GFP signals started to appear in the nucleus.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claims.claim: Within a stage-synchronized population, animals exhibited variable patterns of MYRF-1GFP's localization.
claims.source: Within a stage-synchronized population, animals exhibited variable patterns of MYRF-1GFP's localization, that is primarily at the cell membrane, primarily in the nucleus, or both at the cell membrane and in the nucleus (Figure 4B–F).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 4B–F.

claims.claim: Cell-membrane-to-nucleus transition of MYRF-1GFP was observed in DD neurons.
claims.source: By colabeling with DD-expressing mCherry::Rab-3, we observed cell-membrane-to-nucleus transition of MYRF-1GFP in DD neurons (Figure 4E,F).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 4E,F.

claims.claim: MYRF-2GFP exhibited stronger signals than MYRF-1GFP in early L1 larvae.
claims.source: A similar early-stage cell membrane-localization was observed for MYRF-2GFP, the paralog of MYRF-1, except that MYRF-2GFP exhibited stronger signals than MYRF-1GFP in early L1 larvae (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: MYRF-2GFP displayed the trend of localization transitioning from cell membrane to nucleus during L1 development.
claims.source: MYRF-2GFP also displayed the trend of localization transitioning from cell membrane to nucleus during L1 development.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claims.claim: MYRFGFP is localized primarily at cell membrane in early L1 animals, and becomes increasingly localized in the nucleus as larval development progresses.
claims.source: Together, we observed that MYRFGFP is localized primarily at cell membrane in early L1 animals, and becomes increasingly localized in the nucleus as larval development progresses.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section as a summary of observations.

claims.claim: myrf-1S483A K488A GFP allele caused a larval arrest in animals, similar to the arrest observed in myrf-1 null mutants.
claims.source: This myrf-1S483A K488A GFP allele caused a larval arrest in animals (Figure 5B,C), similar to the arrest observed in myrf-1 null mutants and consistent with our previous finding that myrf-1's activity is cleavage-dependent.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 5B,C.

claims.claim: MYRF-1S483A K488A GFP was only detected at the cell membrane but not in the nucleus at any viable stages.
claims.source: Importantly, MYRF-1S483A K488A GFP was only detected at the cell membrane but not in the nucleus at any viable stages (Figure 5D–G).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 5D–G.

claims.claim: The intensity of MYRF-1S483A K488A GFP was increased compared to wild type.
claims.source: The intensity of MYRF-1S483A K488A GFP was increased compared to wild type, in accordance with our prediction that mutant MYRF would accumulate on cell membrane because it cannot be cleaved.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claims.claim: The overall course of synaptic rewiring in myrf-1S483A K488A GFP was similar to myrf-1(ybq6), a putative null indel allele.
claims.source: The overall course of synaptic rewiring in myrf-1S483A K488A GFP was similar to myrf-1(ybq6), a putative null indel allele, although the synaptic rewiring in myrf-1S483A K488A GFP appeared to be less complete than myrf-1(ybq6) (Figure 6; Figure 6—figure supplements 1–6).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 6 and supplements.

claims.claim: When myrf-2 was simultaneously mutated with myrf-1S483A K488A GFP, the synaptic rewiring was severely blocked.
claims.source: When myrf-2, the paralog of myrf-1, was simultaneously mutated, the synaptic rewiring was severely blocked (Figure 6; Figure 6—figure supplements 7–12), consistent with our previous finding that myrf-1 and myrf-2 are together indispensable for synaptic rewiring in DDs.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 6 and supplements.

claims.claim: MYRF is associated with cell membrane before cleavage, which is temporally controlled during development.
claims.source: These data support that MYRF is associated with cell membrane before cleavage, which is temporally controlled during development.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the loss-of-cleavage mutant analysis.

claims.claim: PAN-1 binding was observed with the C-terminal region of MYRF, but not with the N-terminal region.
claims.source: PAN-1 binding was observed with the C-terminal region of MYRF, but not with the N-terminal region (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 7B showing co-IP results.

claims.claim: PAN-1 may use its non-cytoplasmic LRR domains to interact with the non-cytoplasmic region of MYRF.
claims.source: This result is consistent with their topographic configuration on ER membrane, which predicts that PAN-1 may use its non-cytoplasmic LRR domains to interact with the non-cytoplasmic region of MYRF.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section as an inference from the co-IP results.

claims.claim: The LRR domains of PAN-1 was responsible for binding with C-MYRF.
claims.source: The LRR domains of PAN-1 was responsible for binding with C-MYRF (Figure 7C); the binding occurred when the two fragments coexisted either in the ER lumen or cytoplasm of HEK cells.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 7C.

claims.claim: The cytoplasmic region of PAN-1 was dispensable for PAN-1's binding with MYRF.
claims.source: The cytoplasmic region of PAN-1 was dispensable for PAN-1's binding with MYRF.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claims.claim: PAN-1 uses its LRR domain to interact with the extracellular region of MYRF.
claims.source: Together these data indicate that PAN-1 uses its LRR domain to interact with the extracellular region of MYRF.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from deletion experiments.

claims.claim: myrf-11-700 GFP deletion allele was recessive and homozygous mutants exhibited larval arrest at L2.
claims.source: This deletion allele was recessive and homozygous mutants exhibited larval arrest at L2, indicating that the extracellular domain of MYRF-1 was necessary for normal function (Figure 8B,C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 8B,C.

claims.claim: The extracellular domain of MYRF-1 was necessary for normal function.
claims.source: This deletion allele was recessive and homozygous mutants exhibited larval arrest at L2, indicating that the extracellular domain of MYRF-1 was necessary for normal function (Figure 8B,C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 8B,C.

claims.claim: MYRF-11-700 GFP displayed prominent cytoplasmic signals while its cell-membrane or nuclear localization were not obvious at any viable stages.
claims.source: Importantly, MYRF-11-700 GFP displayed prominent cytoplasmic signals while its cell-membrane or nuclear localization were not obvious at any viable stages (Figure 8D–F; Figure 8—figure supplement 1), showing that the extracellular domain is required for MYRF's proper localization.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 8D–F and supplement.

claims.claim: The extracellular domain is required for MYRF's proper localization.
claims.source: Importantly, MYRF-11-700 GFP displayed prominent cytoplasmic signals while its cell-membrane or nuclear localization were not obvious at any viable stages (Figure 8D–F; Figure 8—figure supplement 1), showing that the extracellular domain is required for MYRF's proper localization.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 8D–F and supplement.

claims.claim: myrf-11-790 GFP mutant displayed larval arrest at L2.
claims.source: myrf-11-790 GFP mutant also displayed larval arrest at L2 (Figure 8B,C) and prominent cytoplasmic GFP signal instead of cell membrane or nuclear signals (Figure 8D–F; Figure 8—figure supplement 1), supporting that that the extracellular region of MYRF is functionally critical.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 8B,C.

claims.claim: The extracellular region of MYRF-2 was necessary for MYRF-2's cell membrane localization.
claims.source: Using a similar strategy, we analyzed an in-frame deletion allele myrf-21-728 GFP and found that the extracellular region of MYRF-2 was necessary for MYRF-2's cell membrane localization because MYRF-21-728 was primarily detected in cytoplasm (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: myrf-11-790 GFP allele exhibited blocked synaptic rewiring under myrf-2 null background.
claims.source: myrf-11-790 GFP allele, in which a part of the extracellular domain of MYRF was removed, exhibited blocked synaptic rewiring under myrf-2 null background (Figure 6; Figure 6—figure supplements 1–12), a phenotype similarly observed in myrf-1(ybq6).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 6 and supplements.

claims.claim: myrf-11-700 GFP allele exhibited precocious synaptic rewiring.
claims.source: In contrast, myrf-11-700 GFP allele, in which the whole extracellular region of MYRF is lost, exhibited precocious synaptic rewiring, that is clearly detectable synaptic puncta formed in the dorsal processes of DDs at 12, 14 post-hatch hours, time points by which synaptic rewiring has not occurred yet in wild type animals (Figure 6; Figure 6—figure supplements 1–12).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 6 and supplements.

claims.claim: The precocious synaptic rewiring in myrf-11-700 GFP allele also occurred in myrf-2(0) background.
claims.source: The precocious synaptic rewiring in myrf-11-700 GFP allele also occurred in myrf-2(0) background.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claims.claim: The precocious dorsal synapses in myrf-11-700 GFP mutants were not uniformly distributed along the dorsal cord.
claims.source: Notably, the precocious dorsal synapses in myrf-11-700 GFP mutants were not uniformly distributed along the dorsal cord, that is in some DDs the remodeling occurred while in the rest the remodeling did not, even though they were in the same animal, implying that the observed precocity in myrf-11-700 GFP mutants was not a strictly regulated event.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claims.claim: myrf-11-700 GFP caused an advancement in M-cell lineage progression at 12, 14, and 16 post-hatch hours.
claims.source: We found that myrf-11-700 GFP caused an advancement in M-cell lineage progression at 12, 14, and 16 post-hatch hours (Figure 9A).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 9A.

claims.claim: This advancement in M-cell lineage was eliminated when myrf-2 was simultaneously mutated.
claims.source: Curiously, this advancement was eliminated when myrf-2 was simultaneously mutated (as a putative indel null); even more so, M-cell division was delayed in myrf-11-700 GFP; myrf-2(0) double mutants (Figure 9A).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 9A.

claims.claim: The synaptic rewiring was normally initiated when the M-cell underwent the 4th M-cell division (8 + cell).
claims.source: By dual-labeling M-cell progenitors and synapses of DDs in the same individuals, we determined that the synaptic rewiring was normally initiated when the M-cell underwent the 4th M-cell division (8 + cell); this coordination of timing was disrupted in myrf-11-700 GFP mutants because many animals had displayed rewired dorsal synapses while only containing less than 4 M-cell progeny cells (Figure 9B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 9B.

claims.claim: The coordination of timing between synaptic rewiring and M-cell division was disrupted in myrf-11-700 GFP mutants.
claims.source: By dual-labeling M-cell progenitors and synapses of DDs in the same individuals, we determined that the synaptic rewiring was normally initiated when the M-cell underwent the 4th M-cell division (8 + cell); this coordination of timing was disrupted in myrf-11-700 GFP mutants because many animals had displayed rewired dorsal synapses while only containing less than 4 M-cell progeny cells (Figure 9B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 9B.

claims.claim: MYRF-11-700 GFP signals were consistently brighter than MYRF-11-790 GFP signals.
claims.source: The first was that MYRF-11-700 GFP signals were consistently brighter than MYRF-11-790 GFP signals although they were both predominantly cytoplasmic (Figure 8G; Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 8G and supplement.

claims.claim: MYRF-11-700 GFP signals were observed in nuclei of many cells.
claims.source: A more striking feature was that the MYRF-11-700 GFP signals were observed in nuclei of many cells, which is especially evident in big nuclei such as those for seam cells, epidermal cells, and intestinal cells.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claims.claim: Similar nuclear GFP signals were not observed in myrf-11-790 GFP mutants.
claims.source: In contrast, similar nuclear GFP signals were not observed in myrf-11-790 GFP mutants.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claims.claim: The distribution of PAN-1GFP in myrf-1(ju1121) mutants was comparable to that in wild type animals.
claims.source: The distribution of PAN-1GFP in myrf-1(ju1121) mutants was comparable to that in wild type animals (Figure 10E; Figure 10—figure supplement 1), indicating that myrf-1 is unlikely to regulate PAN-1's stability or trafficking.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 10E and supplement.

claims.claim: myrf-1 is unlikely to regulate PAN-1's stability or trafficking.
claims.source: The distribution of PAN-1GFP in myrf-1(ju1121) mutants was comparable to that in wild type animals (Figure 10E; Figure 10—figure supplement 1), indicating that myrf-1 is unlikely to regulate PAN-1's stability or trafficking.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section as an inference from the observation.

claims.claim: MYRF-1GFP or MYRF-2GFP signal, both on the membrane and in the nucleus, was barely detected in pan-1 mutants at all stages examined.
claims.source: In stark contrast, MYRF-1GFP or MYRF-2GFP signal, both on the membrane and in the nucleus, was barely detected in pan-1 mutants at all stages examined (Figure 10A; Figure 10—figure supplement 1A), indicating that PAN-1 critically regulates MYRF localization.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 10A and supplement.

claims.claim: PAN-1 critically regulates MYRF localization.
claims.source: In stark contrast, MYRF-1GFP or MYRF-2GFP signal, both on the membrane and in the nucleus, was barely detected in pan-1 mutants at all stages examined (Figure 10A; Figure 10—figure supplement 1A), indicating that PAN-1 critically regulates MYRF localization.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 10A and supplement.

claims.claim: The loss of MYRFGFP in pan-1(0) was not due to failed transcription of myrf genes.
claims.source: The loss of MYRFGFP in pan-1(0) was not due to failed transcription of myrf genes, as myrf-1 and myrf-2 transcript levels were not significantly changed in pan-1(0) mutants (Figure 10B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 10B showing qPCR data.

claims.claim: MYRF proteins are subject to proteasome degradation in the absence of PAN-1.
claims.source: When critical regulators of the proteasome system were knocked down in pan-1(0) animals, MYRFGFP signals re-emerged in many cells, indicating that MYRF proteins are subject to proteasome degradation in the absence of PAN-1.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claims.claim: Restored MYRFGFP in pan-1 mutants was not localized to the cell membrane or nucleus; rather, the signal appeared in ER-like structures in the cytoplasm.
claims.source: Importantly, restored MYRFGFP in pan-1 mutants was not localized to the cell membrane or nucleus; rather, the signal appeared in ER-like structures in the cytoplasm, suggesting that interaction between PAN-1 and MYRF initiates when they are in ER.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claims.claim: Interaction between PAN-1 and MYRF initiates when they are in ER.
claims.source: Importantly, restored MYRFGFP in pan-1 mutants was not localized to the cell membrane or nucleus; rather, the signal appeared in ER-like structures in the cytoplasm, suggesting that interaction between PAN-1 and MYRF initiates when they are in ER.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section as an inference from the observation.

claims.claim: PAN-1 is necessary for normal localization and function of MYRF.
claims.source: In conclusion, PAN-1 is necessary for normal localization and function of MYRF.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion.

claims.claim: Exogenously expressed pan-1 can restore the cell-membrane localization of MYRF in pan-1 mutants.
claims.source: We used a seam cell-specific promoter to drive pan-1 expression (Figure 10D) and observed restored nuclear MYRF-1GFP signal in seam cells of pan-1(0) animals, indicating that MYRF had been normally localized and processed in those cells.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 10D.

claims.claim: MYRF-11-700 GFP signals remained strong in pan-1(0) mutants.
claims.source: The prediction proved to be correct because MYRF-11-700 GFP signals remained strong in pan-1(0) mutants (Figure 10F).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 10F.

claims.claim: The signals of MYRF-11-790 GFP were undetectable in pan-1(0).
claims.source: In contrast, the signals of MYRF-11-790 GFP, in which part of extracellular region was removed, were undetectable in pan-1(0), resembling wild-type MYRF in pan-1(0).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claims.claim: PAN-1 is essential for stabilizing MYRF and trafficking it to cell membrane.
claims.source: Therefore, PAN-1 is essential for stabilizing MYRF and trafficking it to cell membrane.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion.

claims.claim: Overexpression of the extracellular region of MYRF-1 in DD neurons blocked synaptic remodeling.
claims.source: Overexpression of either fusion protein (TMD::MYRF-1681-931 and SP:: MYRF-1681-931) in DD neurons blocked synaptic remodeling, supporting that the interaction between PAN-1 and MYRF is important for MYRF activity.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claims.claim: The interaction between PAN-1 and MYRF is important for MYRF activity.
claims.source: Overexpression of either fusion protein (TMD::MYRF-1681-931 and SP:: MYRF-1681-931) in DD neurons blocked synaptic remodeling, supporting that the interaction between PAN-1 and MYRF is important for MYRF activity.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from overexpression experiments.

claims.claim: ER-retained PAN-1 impeded the rewiring processes drastically.
claims.source: The ER-retained PAN-1 indeed impeded the rewiring processes drastically, as the dorsal synapses were greatly reduced and most of the juvenile ventral synapses were sustained by 28 post-hatch hours.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claims.claim: When ER-retained PAN-1 was expressed in DDs and seam cells, MYRFGFP signals were primarily cytoplasmic showing a pattern similar to ER structures.
claims.source: When ER-retained PAN-1 was expressed in DDs as well as seam cells of animals carrying myrf-1GFP, we observed much brighter MYRFGFP signals in target cells than in neighbor cells, and importantly, the signals were primarily cytoplasmic showing a pattern similar to ER structures.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claims.claim: PAN-1 promotes MYRF's transport to cell membrane.
claims.source: These results support that PAN-1 promotes MYRF's transport to cell membrane, and that PAN-1 interacting with MYRF in ER is insufficient for MYRF's cleavage.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from ER-retention experiments.

claims.claim: PAN-1 interacting with MYRF in ER is insufficient for MYRF's cleavage.
claims.source: These results support that PAN-1 promotes MYRF's transport to cell membrane, and that PAN-1 interacting with MYRF in ER is insufficient for MYRF's cleavage.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from ER-retention experiments.

claims.claim: MYRF-11-482 GFP concentrated in the nucleus throughout the body.
claims.source: This mutant MYRF-11-482 GFP concentrated in the nucleus throughout the body (Figure 12; Figure 12—figure supplement 1), consistent with N-MYRF possessing a nuclear localization signal and nuclear function (Li et al., 2013; Meng et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 12 and supplement.

claims.claim: Despite MYRF-11-482 GFP nuclear localization, the mutants arrested at L2, similar to the myrf-1 null allele.
claims.source: However, despite MYRF-11-482 GFP nuclear localization, the mutants arrested at L2, similar to the myrf-1 null allele, indicating that N-MYRF alone cannot substitute for full-length MYRF.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claims.claim: N-MYRF alone cannot substitute for full-length MYRF.
claims.source: However, despite MYRF-11-482 GFP nuclear localization, the mutants arrested at L2, similar to the myrf-1 null allele, indicating that N-MYRF alone cannot substitute for full-length MYRF.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion.

claims.claim: In myrf-11-656 GFP mutant, GFP-MYRF-11-656 accumulated in nuclei throughout the body at all viable stages, but the animals displayed larval arrest similar to that in myrf-1 null animals.
claims.source: In this mutant, GFP-MYRF-11-656 accumulated in nuclei throughout the body at all viable stages, but the animals displayed larval arrest similar to that in myrf-1 null animals.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claims.claim: The synaptic rewiring in both myrf-11-482 GFP and myrf-11-656 GFP showed deficiency similar to myrf-1(ybq6).
claims.source: The synaptic rewiring in both myrf-11-482 GFP and myrf-11-656 GFP showed deficiency similar to myrf-1(ybq6) (Figure 6; Figure 6—figure supplements 1–12)
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 6 and supplements.

claims.claim: MYRF membrane-association is indispensable for MYRF's function.
claims.source: Therefore, the analysis of the two N-MYRF-only mutants support that MYRF membrane-association is indispensable for MYRF's function (Figure 13).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion and supported by Figure 13.

claims.claim: MYRF is subcellularly localized on the cell membrane in animal development for the first time.
claims.source: Our results, for the first time, show that MYRF is subcellularly localized on the cell membrane in animal development.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion section.

claims.claim: PAN-1 is required for proper function of MYRF.
claims.source: Our results demonstrate that PAN-1 is required for proper function of MYRF.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion section.

claims.claim: The extracellular domain of PAN-1 is highly homologous to the ectodomain of human Toll-like receptor 5 (TLR5).
claims.source: The extracellular domain of PAN-1 is highly homologous to the ectodomain of human Toll-like receptor 5 (TLR5), a member of the toll-like receptor (TLR) family (Dolan et al., 2007; Gissendanner and Kelley, 2013).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with citation.

claims.claim: TLR5 is known to recognize bacterial flagellin to initiate an intracellular signaling cascade in innate immunity response.
claims.source: TLR5 is known to recognize bacterial flagellin to initiate an intracellular signaling cascade in innate immunity response (Hayashi et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with citation.

claims.claim: Tmem98 has been identified as a MYRF interactor in both C. elegans and mouse.
claims.source: One factor, Tmem98, has been identified as a MYRF interactor in both C. elegans and mouse (Huang et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with citation.

claims.claim: The two proteins' interaction on the membrane inhibits MYRF cleavage in human cell lines.
claims.source: The two proteins' interaction on the membrane inhibits MYRF cleavage in human cell lines.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion section.

claims.claim: The non-cytoplasmic part of MYRF protein is indispensable for its function.

claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion section.

claims.source: Previous in vitro studies demonstrated that truncated human MYRF(1-756), lacking the transmembrane domain and non-cytoplasmic region, was much less competent at promoting oligodendrocyte maturation than full-length MYRF, even though the truncated MYRF(1-756), when overexpressed, can be processed to release N-MYRF in cultured cells (Li et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with citation.

claims.source: Two recent human genetics studies identified that haplotypes of MYRF C-terminal variants can cause nanophthalmos, a potentially devastating eye condition (Rossetti et al., 2019; Siggs et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with citation.

claims.source: However, in present study, endogenous expression of N-MYRF (as in myrf-11-482 GFP, myrf-11-656 GFP) appeared to be deficient in MYRF function, even though N-MYRF-1 in all cases concentrated in the nucleus.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion section.

claims.claim: Full-length MYRF-1 could rescue the defective synaptic rewiring in myrf-1; myrf-2 double mutants, while N-MYRF-1 could not.
claims.source: We found that the full-length MYRF-1 could rescue the defective synaptic rewiring in myrf-1; myrf-2 double mutants, while N-MYRF-1 could not (Figure 12—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and supported by Figure 12—figure supplement 2.

results.result: PAN-1, a leucine-rich-repeat domain transmembrane protein, was identified as a binding partner of MYRF-1 and MYRF-2 through IP-MS analysis and co-immunoprecipitation experiments, indicating that MYRF and PAN-1 can form a protein complex in vivo and likely interact directly.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C35 provide converging evidence from multiple independent approaches (IP-MS in both directions and co-IP in heterologous cells) demonstrating the physical interaction between PAN-1 and MYRF proteins. The use of reciprocal IP-MS and validation in human cells strengthens the conclusion of direct interaction.

results.result: Loss of pan-1 results in defective synaptic remodeling in DD neurons, with few dorsal synapses forming by late L1 and the defect persisting through L2, while general synaptogenesis remains intact as evidenced by the presence of juvenile ventral synapses.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C41 are supported by quantitative imaging data showing reduced dorsal synapse formation in pan-1 mutants (Figure 1D,E) while ventral synapses remain present. The temporal analysis and morphological controls strengthen the conclusion that pan-1 specifically affects synaptic remodeling rather than general synaptogenesis.

results.result: PAN-1B, the longest transmembrane isoform of PAN-1, regulates synaptic remodeling in DD neurons cell-autonomously, as demonstrated by rescue experiments showing that expression of pan-1b, but not pan-1a or pan-1c, in DD neurons restores synaptic remodeling in pan-1 mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C47 are supported by systematic rescue experiments testing different isoforms and tissue-specific expression patterns (Figure 2B and supplements). The demonstration that DD-specific expression is sufficient for rescue while expression in other tissues is not provides strong evidence for cell-autonomous function.

results.result: PAN-1 localizes to the cell membrane in various cell types including DD neurons, seam cells, and ventral cord neurons, with this membrane localization and the extracellular LRR domains being essential for its function in synaptic remodeling.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C55 are supported by colocalization studies with membrane markers (Figure 3B-D) and functional deletion analysis (Figure 3E). The demonstration that deletion of either the signal peptide or transmembrane domain abolishes function, while the cytoplasmic region is dispensable, provides strong evidence for the importance of membrane localization and extracellular domains.

results.result: MYRF-1 localizes primarily at the cell membrane in early L1 larvae and progressively transitions to nuclear localization during L1 development, with this cell-membrane-to-nucleus transition observed in DD neurons and coinciding with the timing of synaptic rewiring.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C62 are supported by time-course imaging of MYRF-1GFP knock-in animals showing the developmental transition from membrane to nuclear localization (Figure 4B-F). The quantification of localization patterns across developmental stages and colocalization with DD markers provides strong evidence for the temporal regulation of MYRF localization.

results.result: A loss-of-cleavage mutant of MYRF-1 (S483A K488A) accumulates at the cell membrane without nuclear localization and causes larval arrest similar to null mutants, demonstrating that MYRF is associated with cell membrane before cleavage and that this process is temporally controlled during development.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C68 are supported by analysis of a rationally designed cleavage-deficient mutant showing membrane accumulation without nuclear localization (Figure 5D-G) and phenotypic analysis showing developmental arrest and synaptic rewiring defects (Figure 5B,C and Figure 6). The consistency between predicted and observed localization patterns strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: PAN-1 and MYRF interact via their extracellular regions, with the LRR domains of PAN-1 binding to the C-terminal extracellular region of MYRF, while the cytoplasmic region of PAN-1 is dispensable for this interaction.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C73 are supported by systematic co-IP experiments in HEK293T cells testing different domain deletions (Figure 7B,C). The demonstration that PAN-1 binds the C-terminal but not N-terminal region of MYRF, and that the LRR domains are necessary and sufficient for binding, provides strong evidence for the domain-specific interaction.

results.result: The extracellular domain of MYRF is necessary for its proper localization and normal function, as demonstrated by in-frame deletion mutants that exhibit prominent cytoplasmic localization instead of cell membrane or nuclear localization, along with larval arrest phenotypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C79 are supported by analysis of multiple deletion alleles (myrf-1^1-700 and myrf-1^1-790) showing loss of proper localization and developmental arrest (Figure 8B-F). The consistency of phenotypes across different deletions and between MYRF-1 and MYRF-2 strengthens the conclusion about the functional importance of the extracellular domain.

results.result: The myrf-1^1-700 deletion mutant, lacking the entire extracellular domain, exhibits precocious and discordant synaptic rewiring that is not uniformly distributed and disrupts the normal coordination between synaptic rewiring and M-cell division timing.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C87 are supported by detailed temporal analysis of synaptic rewiring and M-cell division in deletion mutants (Figure 6 and Figure 9). The demonstration of precocious rewiring at early time points and loss of coordination with M-cell division provides strong evidence for aberrant developmental timing. However, the mechanistic basis for the precocity remains unclear.

results.result: Loss of PAN-1 abolishes MYRF cell membrane and nuclear localization, leading to proteasome-mediated degradation of MYRF in the ER, demonstrating that PAN-1 is necessary for MYRF stabilization, trafficking to the cell membrane, and subsequent nuclear translocation.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C99 are supported by multiple lines of evidence including loss of MYRF-GFP signal in pan-1 mutants (Figure 10A), unchanged myrf transcript levels (Figure 10B), restoration of ER-localized MYRF upon proteasome inhibition (Figure 10C), and cell-type-specific rescue (Figure 10D). The convergence of genetic, cell biological, and biochemical evidence strongly supports the conclusion.

results.result: MYRF-1^1-700, which lacks the extracellular domain, remains stable in pan-1 mutants while MYRF-1^1-790, which retains part of the extracellular domain, is degraded, demonstrating that PAN-1 is essential for stabilizing MYRF through interaction with its extracellular domain.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C103 are supported by differential stability analysis of MYRF deletion variants in pan-1 mutants (Figure 10F). The observation that complete removal of the extracellular domain confers PAN-1-independent stability while partial deletion does not provides strong evidence for the domain-specific requirement for PAN-1-mediated stabilization.

results.result: The interaction between PAN-1 and MYRF on the cell membrane is functionally important for MYRF activity, as demonstrated by dominant-negative effects of overexpressing the MYRF extracellular domain and ER retention of PAN-1, both of which block synaptic remodeling and trap MYRF in the ER.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C109 are supported by functional interference experiments showing that overexpression of MYRF extracellular fragments or ER-retained PAN-1 blocks synaptic remodeling and alters MYRF localization (Figure 11). The consistency of phenotypes from two independent approaches strengthens the conclusion about the functional importance of the PAN-1-MYRF interaction on the membrane.

results.result: N-terminal MYRF fragments (MYRF-1^1-482 and MYRF-1^1-656) that localize to the nucleus are insufficient for MYRF function, as demonstrated by larval arrest and defective synaptic rewiring despite nuclear localization, indicating that MYRF membrane association is indispensable for its function.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C115 are supported by analysis of N-terminal deletion mutants showing nuclear localization but loss of function (Figure 12). The demonstration that nuclear-localized N-MYRF, even with the trimerization domain intact, cannot rescue function provides strong evidence that membrane association is required beyond simply releasing N-MYRF. This is further supported by rescue experiments showing full-length MYRF can rescue while N-MYRF cannot (Figure 12—supplement 2).

results.result: This study provides the first demonstration that MYRF is subcellularly localized on the cell membrane in animal development, with the timing of N-MYRF release from the membrane coinciding with the onset of synaptic rewiring.
results.evaluation: Claims C6 and C116 are supported by the temporal imaging data showing MYRF membrane localization in early L1 and nuclear translocation at late L1 (Figure 4). While the claim of being 'first' cannot be fully verified without comprehensive literature review, the authors provide evidence that previous studies in cultured cells did not describe membrane localization, and the temporal correlation with synaptic rewiring is well-documented.

results.result: The distribution of PAN-1 is not affected by loss of myrf-1, indicating that myrf-1 does not regulate PAN-1 stability or trafficking, suggesting a unidirectional regulatory relationship where PAN-1 regulates MYRF but not vice versa.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C92 are supported by imaging and quantification of PAN-1GFP in myrf-1 mutants showing no significant difference from wild type (Figure 10E and supplement). This establishes the directionality of the regulatory relationship, though the sample size and statistical analysis could be more robust.

results.result: MYRF-1^1-700 signals are consistently brighter than MYRF-1^1-790 signals and show nuclear localization in some cells, while MYRF-1^1-790 does not show nuclear signals, suggesting differential processing or stability of these variants.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C90 are supported by comparative imaging and intensity analysis of the two deletion variants (Figure 8G and supplement). The differential localization patterns are consistent with the functional differences observed in synaptic rewiring assays, though the mechanistic basis for the differences requires further investigation.

results.result: Exogenously expressed pan-1 can restore MYRF cell-membrane localization and nuclear translocation in pan-1 mutants in a cell-type-specific manner, as demonstrated by seam cell-specific expression restoring nuclear MYRF-1GFP in those cells.
results.evaluation: Claim C100 is supported by cell-type-specific rescue experiments showing restoration of nuclear MYRF signals in seam cells expressing exogenous pan-1 (Figure 10D). This provides additional evidence for the cell-autonomous function of PAN-1 in regulating MYRF localization.

results.result: MYRF-2, the paralog of MYRF-1, exhibits similar developmental regulation of subcellular localization, transitioning from cell membrane to nucleus during L1 development, though with stronger signals than MYRF-1 in early L1.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C61 are supported by imaging of MYRF-2GFP showing similar localization patterns to MYRF-1GFP (Figure 4—supplement 1). The consistency between paralogs strengthens the conclusion that this is a conserved regulatory mechanism, though the functional significance of the intensity difference is unclear.

results.result: Background information on DD neuron synaptic rewiring, MYRF family proteins, and their known functions in various organisms, establishing the context for the current study.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C30 represent established knowledge from prior work, appropriately cited throughout. These claims provide necessary context but are not novel findings of this study. The citations appear appropriate and the characterization of prior work is consistent with the cited literature.

results.result: Characterization of normal synaptic remodeling timing and pan-1 expression patterns, providing baseline information for interpreting mutant phenotypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C36, C39, and C42 provide descriptive information about wild-type development and gene expression patterns, supported by imaging data and citations to prior work. These are important controls and baseline observations but represent descriptive rather than mechanistic findings.

results.result: Discussion points relating the current findings to prior work on MYRF function, TLR5 homology, Tmem98 interaction, and human genetic variants, providing broader context for the findings.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C124 represent discussion points connecting the current findings to prior literature. These are appropriately cited and provide important context, though they represent interpretation and synthesis rather than new experimental findings. The connections drawn are reasonable but some are speculative.

results.result: Comparison of overexpression versus endogenous expression of N-MYRF showing that while overexpressed N-MYRF can drive precocious rewiring, endogenously expressed N-MYRF is insufficient for function, suggesting that expression level or oligomerization state affects activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C127 are supported by comparison of prior overexpression data with current endogenous expression data from deletion mutants (Figure 12—supplement 2). The interpretation that trimerization efficiency may differ between overexpressed and endogenous N-MYRF is reasonable but remains speculative without direct biochemical evidence.

results.result: Prior knowledge that full-length MYRF undergoes self-cleavage on ER membrane in cultured cells and that MYRF is a membrane-bound transcription factor indispensable for synaptic rewiring.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C4 represent established knowledge from prior work that is appropriately cited. These provide important context for understanding why the current findings of cell membrane localization and regulated cleavage in vivo are significant departures from the cultured cell model.
